content.text: Chapter 4 asks what governs the motion of bodies. Everyday examples suggest that forces can start, stop, speed up, slow down, or redirect motion. Forces may arise through contact, such as a kick or wind, or act at a distance, such as gravity and magnetic attraction. The chapter investigates whether a force is needed to maintain uniform motion.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Introduction to laws of motion

content.text: Aristotle proposed that an external force is required to keep a body moving. This seems plausible because moving objects on Earth eventually stop. The chapter explains that this occurs because friction and viscous forces oppose motion. A child must pull a toy car to overcome friction; without friction, no continuing push would be needed to maintain uniform motion.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Aristotle’s fallacy

content.text: Galileo studied objects on inclined planes. Objects moving downhill accelerate and those moving uphill retard. On a frictionless horizontal plane, an object would move with constant velocity. In a double-inclined-plane experiment, a ball climbs nearly to its starting height; as the second plane becomes less steep, it travels farther to reach that height. In the limiting horizontal case, it would continue indefinitely if friction were absent.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Galileo and the law of inertia

content.text: Inertia is the property of a body by which it resists a change in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion. Rest and uniform linear motion are equivalent in the sense that both have zero acceleration. Friction often hides this principle in everyday experience.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Inertia

content.text: Every body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by an external force to act otherwise. Equivalently, if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero. Conversely, non-zero acceleration requires a non-zero net external force.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Newton’s first law of motion

content.text: A book resting on a horizontal table experiences its weight downward and the table’s normal reaction upward. Because the book is observed to be at rest, the first law implies that the net external force is zero, so the normal reaction equals the weight in this situation. It is incorrect to argue that equal forces cause rest; the observed state of motion is what allows the first law to infer zero net force.
equations: R = W (for a book at rest on a horizontal table)

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: First law and balanced forces

content.text: When a stationary bus starts suddenly, a passenger tends to remain in the original state of rest, so relative to the bus the passenger appears to fall backward. When a moving bus stops suddenly, the passenger’s body tends to continue moving forward. Friction between the feet and floor and muscular forces subsequently change the body’s motion. A car accelerates because an external frictional force from the road acts on it; at constant velocity the net external force is zero.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Inertia in buses and cars

content.text: An astronaut separates from a spaceship accelerating in interstellar space at 100 m s⁻². Assuming no nearby stars exert a gravitational force and the spaceship’s gravitational attraction is negligible, the net force on the astronaut after separation is zero. By Newton’s first law, the astronaut’s acceleration immediately after separation is zero.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.1: astronaut separated from spaceship

content.text: The momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity. Momentum is a vector quantity and has the direction of velocity. A heavier body or a faster body generally requires a larger force to bring about the same momentum change in the same time.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Momentum

content.text: The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the applied net external force and takes place in the direction of that force. In SI units the proportionality constant is chosen as one. For constant mass, the net external force equals mass times acceleration. The SI unit of force is the newton, where one newton produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in a mass of 1 kg.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Newton’s second law of motion

content.text: Newton’s second law is a vector equation and can be expressed separately along the x, y and z directions. A force changes the velocity component along its direction; the component normal to the force remains unchanged when no force acts in that direction. In projectile motion under gravity alone, the horizontal velocity component remains constant.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Vector nature and component form of the second law

content.text: For a system of particles or a rigid body, the force in the second law is the total external force on the system and the acceleration is that of the system as a whole (the centre of mass). Internal forces are not included in the total external force. The second law is local: the force acting at a particular place and instant determines the acceleration at that place and instant, rather than depending on the past history of motion.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Second law for systems and local relation

content.text: A 0.04 kg bullet enters a wooden block at 90 m s⁻¹ and stops after 0.60 m. Assuming constant retardation, use v² = u² + 2as to obtain a = −6750 m s⁻². The magnitude of the average retarding force is m|a| = 270 N. The text notes that the actual resistive force may not be uniform, so this result represents an average.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.2: resistive force on a bullet

content.text: For a particle whose position coordinate is y = ut + ½gt², differentiation gives velocity v = u + gt and acceleration a = g. Therefore the force is F = mg, in the direction of g.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.3: force from a position equation

content.text: Impulse is the product of force and the time interval during which it acts, and equals the change in momentum. It is useful when a large force acts for a short time, such as a ball bouncing off a wall. An impulsive force is not a fundamentally different kind of force; it is simply a large force acting briefly.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Impulse

content.text: A batsman sends a 0.15 kg ball back toward the bowler without changing its speed of 12 m s⁻¹. Taking the initial direction toward the batsman as positive, the momentum changes from +mv to −mv, so the magnitude of impulse is 2mv = 3.6 N s, directed from the batsman toward the bowler.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.4: impulse imparted by a batsman

content.text: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. More precisely, the force on body A by body B equals the negative of the force on body B by A. The two forces act simultaneously on different bodies; neither is the cause of the other. They cannot cancel when considering one body alone. They are internal forces and cancel in pairs when considering the combined two-body system.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Newton’s third law

content.text: Two identical billiard balls strike a rigid wall at the same speed but at different angles and rebound without changing speed. The wall’s force on each ball is normal to the wall because only the normal component of momentum changes. For a normal impact, impulse magnitude is 2mu; for an impact at 30° to the normal, it is 2mu cos 30°. The ratio of magnitudes for the first and second cases is 2/√3 ≈ 1.2. By the third law, the force on the wall is opposite to the force on the ball.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.5: billiard balls and a wall

content.text: The second and third laws imply conservation of momentum for an isolated system. Internal forces between interacting particles change individual momenta by equal and opposite amounts, so the total momentum remains unchanged. For a gun and bullet initially at rest, the bullet’s momentum and the gun’s recoil momentum are equal and opposite. Momentum conservation applies to elastic and inelastic collisions; elastic collisions additionally conserve total kinetic energy.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Conservation of momentum

content.text: A particle is in equilibrium when the net external force on it is zero; it is then at rest or moves with uniform velocity. For two forces, they must be equal and opposite. For three concurrent forces, their vector sum must be zero and they can be represented by the sides of a triangle taken in the same sense. More generally, forces in equilibrium can be represented by a closed polygon. Equilibrium of an extended body also requires rotational equilibrium, discussed later in the textbook.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Equilibrium of a particle

content.text: A 6 kg mass hangs from a massless rope and a 50 N horizontal force is applied at the rope’s midpoint. The weight is T₂ = mg = 60 N. At the midpoint, equilibrium gives T₁ cos θ = 60 N and T₁ sin θ = 50 N, so tan θ = 50/60. The angle does not depend on rope length or on where along the rope the horizontal force is applied under the stated assumptions.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.6: mass suspended by a rope with horizontal force

content.text: Gravity acts at a distance and is pervasive in mechanics. Most other forces discussed in ordinary mechanics are contact forces arising when bodies touch, including normal reaction, friction, buoyancy, viscous force and air resistance. The normal reaction is the component of contact force perpendicular to the contacting surfaces; friction is the component parallel to them. At the microscopic level, contact forces ultimately arise from electrical interactions between charged constituents.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Common forces: gravity and contact forces

content.text: A spring produces a restoring force when compressed or extended. For small displacements, the force is proportional to displacement from the unstretched state and opposite in direction. The tension in a string is the restoring force associated with an inextensible string; for a string of negligible mass, a constant tension is commonly assumed throughout it.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Spring force and tension

content.text: Static friction opposes impending relative motion between surfaces. It is self-adjusting: it increases to match the applied tangential force up to a limiting value. It is absent when no applied force tends to cause relative motion. The maximum static friction is approximately proportional to the normal force and depends on the pair of surfaces; it is approximately independent of contact area.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Static friction

content.text: When a body begins to slide, kinetic friction opposes relative motion. Its magnitude is approximately μ_k N, is nearly independent of speed and contact area, and the coefficient μ_k is usually smaller than μ_s. For a body pulled by a force F while sliding, acceleration is (F − f_k)/m along the pull direction. If the applied force is removed, friction causes retardation.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Kinetic or sliding friction

content.text: For a block at rest on an inclined plane of angle θ, the component of weight down the plane is mg sin θ and the normal force is mg cos θ. Static friction balances the downslope component while the block remains at rest. At the limiting angle θmax, static friction reaches μsN, giving tan θmax = μs. The limiting angle is independent of the block’s mass.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Friction on an inclined plane

content.text: A box remains stationary relative to a train only if static friction can provide its acceleration. Since ma ≤ μsN = μsmg, the maximum acceleration is amax = μsg. With μs = 0.15 and g = 10 m s⁻², amax = 1.5 m s⁻².

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.7: maximum acceleration of a train

content.text: A 4 kg block just begins to slide when a horizontal plane is inclined to 15°. At the limiting angle, tan θmax = μs, so μs = tan 15° ≈ 0.27. The result does not depend on the block’s mass.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.8: coefficient of static friction from an incline

content.text: A 3 kg hanging block pulls a 20 kg trolley on a horizontal surface with μk = 0.04 and g = 10 m s⁻². For the hanging block, 30 − T = 3a. For the trolley, T − fk = 20a, with fk = μkN = 0.04 × 200 = 8 N. Solving gives a = 22/23 ≈ 0.96 m s⁻² and T ≈ 27.1 N.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.9: block and trolley with kinetic friction

content.text: In ideal rolling without slipping, the point of contact is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface, so friction may be zero in the idealised case. In practice, deformation creates rolling resistance, which is much smaller than static or sliding friction for the same weight. Lubricants, ball bearings and a cushion of air can reduce friction and energy dissipation. Friction is also useful: brakes depend on it, and tyre-road friction lets vehicles accelerate; static friction enables walking.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Rolling friction and reducing friction

content.text: A body moving at uniform speed in a circle requires inward centripetal acceleration v²/R and hence an inward force mv²/R. Centripetal force is not a separate fundamental kind of force; it is the name for the net inward force supplied by a material interaction such as tension, gravity or friction. For a car on a level road, static friction provides the centripetal force, with N = mg. The no-skid condition is v² ≤ μsRg.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Centripetal force on a level road

content.text: Banking a road allows the horizontal component of the normal reaction to contribute to centripetal force and reduces reliance on friction. At the optimum speed, friction is not needed and v₀ = √(Rg tan θ). With friction, the maximum speed depends on R, g, banking angle θ and μs. The chapter’s equations resolve forces into vertical and horizontal components and use the limiting friction f = μsN for the maximum permissible speed.
equations: N cos θ = mg + f sin θ
N sin θ + f cos θ = mv²/R

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Circular motion on a banked road

content.text: For a cyclist on an unbanked road, friction must provide the centripetal force. The no-slip condition is v² ≤ μsRg. With R = 3 m, g = 9.8 m s⁻² and μs = 0.1, μsRg = 2.94 m² s⁻². A speed of 18 km h⁻¹ = 5 m s⁻¹ gives v² = 25 m² s⁻², which exceeds the limit, so the cyclist slips.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.10: cyclist on a circular turn

content.text: A circular racetrack of radius 300 m is banked at 15°, with coefficient of friction 0.2. At the optimum speed, the normal reaction alone supplies the centripetal force, so v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) ≈ 28.1 m s⁻¹. The maximum permissible speed is found from the chapter’s banked-road relation using limiting friction f = μsN.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.11: banked racetrack

content.text: To solve mechanics problems systematically: draw a schematic of bodies and connections; choose the part to treat as the system; draw a free-body diagram showing every force acting on that system from the environment; include known magnitudes and directions and treat the rest as unknowns; and, if analysing another body, apply Newton’s third law to show the mutual force with equal magnitude and opposite direction. Do not include forces exerted by the system on its environment in the system’s free-body diagram.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: System selection and free-body diagrams

content.text: A 2 kg block rests on a soft floor. A 25 kg cylinder is placed on it, and then the block-cylinder system accelerates downward at 0.1 m s⁻²; take g = 10 m s⁻². Before the floor yields, the floor’s upward normal force on the block is 20 N, so the block’s force on the floor is 20 N downward. After yielding, the system’s weight is 270 N and 270 − R′ = 27 × 0.1, giving R′ = 267.3 N; the system pushes downward on the floor with 267.3 N. Action-reaction pairs act on different bodies; weight and normal force on the same body are not a third-law pair.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Worked example 4.12: block and cylinder on a yielding floor

content.text: The chapter summary states that Aristotle’s view of force needed for uniform motion is wrong because friction opposes motion. Galileo’s law of inertia became Newton’s first law. Momentum is p = mv; Newton’s second law is F = dp/dt = ma in SI units, with 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻². Impulse equals change in momentum. Newton’s third law describes equal and opposite simultaneous mutual forces acting on different bodies.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Summary: Newton’s laws, momentum and impulse

content.text: The total momentum of an isolated system is conserved. Static friction opposes impending relative motion and satisfies fs ≤ μsN; kinetic friction opposes actual relative motion and is approximately fk = μkN. The coefficients depend on the contacting surfaces, and experiments find μk < μs.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Summary: momentum conservation and friction

content.text: The force need not point in the direction of motion; it is parallel to acceleration and may point along, opposite to, or normal to velocity. At an instant when velocity is zero, force and acceleration need not be zero, as for a ball at its highest point. Force depends on the situation at that instant, not on the body’s earlier motion. In F = ma, ma is not an additional force besides the net external force.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to ponder: force and motion

content.text: Centripetal force is a role played by an actual force, not a new kind of force. Static friction is self-adjusting up to μsN; do not set fs = μsN unless the limiting value is reached. The relation mg = R applies to a body on a table only in equilibrium. Action and reaction are simultaneous mutual forces on different bodies. Terms such as friction, normal reaction, tension, air resistance, viscous drag, thrust, buoyancy, weight and centripetal force should be understood as a force on one body by another. Walking requires external friction.
